facts: Every **square** is also a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram and a kite.
Every **rectangle** and every **rhombus** is also a parallelogram.
Every **rhombus** is also a **kite**, because four equal sides include two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
Inclusion runs **one way only**: every square is a rhombus, but only some rhombuses are squares.
The **most specific name** is the lowest name in the hierarchy that the shape fits; the more general names are still true.
steps: Write down the properties the shape is known to have.
Write down the properties the claimed name requires.
The shape has that name only if it has every property the name requires.

foundation.solution_text:
The four corner marks show that all four angles are right angles, and the ticks show that opposite sides are equal.
Opposite sides equal and parallel make it a parallelogram, and the right angles make it a rectangle.
The adjacent sides carry different ticks, so it is not a rhombus and not a square.
Quadrilateral, parallelogram, rectangle

All four sides carry the same tick and both pairs of opposite sides are marked parallel, so the shape is a rhombus.
Both pairs of opposite sides parallel make it a parallelogram, and the two pairs of equal adjacent sides make it a kite.
No right angle is marked, so it need not be a square.
Quadrilateral, kite, parallelogram, rhombus

Only one pair of opposite sides carries the parallel arrows, so the shape is a trapezium.
A parallelogram needs a second pair of parallel sides, so the rhombus and the rectangle are ruled out with it.
Quadrilateral, trapezium

A kite needs two pairs of equal adjacent sides, and there are no equal sides at all.
A trapezium needs a pair of parallel sides, and a parallelogram and a rectangle need two pairs, but there are no parallel sides.
Quadrilateral

foundation.question_text: A square is a type of rhombus. Is this always true? Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
A rhombus is a quadrilateral with four equal sides.
Every square has four equal sides, so every square has the property a rhombus needs.
Yes, this is always true.

foundation.question_text: A parallelogram is a type of square. Is this always true? Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
A square needs four equal sides and four right angles.
A parallelogram is only guaranteed to have its opposite sides equal and parallel, so it need not have either of those properties.
No — a parallelogram is a square only in the special case where all four sides are equal and all four angles are right angles.

foundation.question_text: Explain why every square is also a rectangle.
foundation.solution_text:
A rectangle is a quadrilateral with opposite sides equal and four right angles.
A square has opposite sides equal, and all four of its angles are right angles.
A square has every property a rectangle requires, so every square is also a rectangle.

All four angles are marked as right angles, so the shape is a rectangle and Tom is correct.
Four right angles also force both pairs of opposite sides to be parallel, so it is a parallelogram and Katie is correct.
Both are correct, because a rectangle is a special type of parallelogram.

development.solution_text:

A rectangle needs four right angles, and none is marked here, so the shape does not have to be a rectangle.
Only Priya is correct.

The two pairs of equal sides sit next to each other, so the shape is a kite and Sam is correct.
A rhombus needs all four sides equal, but the single ticks and the double ticks mark two different lengths.
Only Sam is correct.

All four sides carry the same double tick, so the shape is a rhombus.
Four equal sides include two pairs of equal adjacent sides, so it is a kite and Sam is correct.
Both pairs of opposite sides are marked parallel, so it is a parallelogram and Priya is correct.
Both are correct, because a rhombus sits below both the kite and the parallelogram in the hierarchy.

development.question_text: A rhombus is a type of kite. Is this always true? Justify your answer from the definition of a kite.
development.solution_text:
A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so the two sides meeting at one vertex are equal and the two sides meeting at the opposite vertex are equal.
That is two pairs of equal adjacent sides, so every rhombus has the property a kite needs.
Yes, this is always true.

development.question_text: Explain why a rectangle is not a type of square.
development.solution_text:
A square needs four right angles and four equal sides.
A rectangle has the four right angles, but its adjacent sides may be different lengths, so it does not have every property a square requires.
A rectangle is a square only in the special case where all four of its sides happen to be equal, so "a rectangle is a square" is not always true.

development.question_text: A quadrilateral is a rectangle, and it is also a rhombus. Name the most specific type it must be, and justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
Being a rectangle gives the shape four right angles.
Being a rhombus gives the shape four equal sides.
A quadrilateral with four right angles and four equal sides is a square.

development.question_text: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram, and it is also a kite. Name the most specific type it must be, and justify your answer.
development.solution_text:
Being a kite gives the shape two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
Being a parallelogram makes the opposite sides equal, so the two pairs must also be equal to each other.
All four sides are then equal, so the quadrilateral is a rhombus.

development.question_text: A quadrilateral has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, and all four of its sides are equal. From the list **quadrilateral, kite, parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square**, write every name that must be given to it.
development.solution_text:
Both pairs of opposite sides parallel make it a parallelogram, and four equal sides then make it a rhombus.
Four equal sides also give two pairs of equal adjacent sides, so it is a kite.
Nothing here forces a right angle, so it need not be a rectangle and need not be a square.
Quadrilateral, kite, parallelogram, rhombus

mastery.question_text:
Decide whether each statement is always true, sometimes true or never true, and give a reason for each.
(a) A rectangle is a rhombus.
(b) A rhombus is a parallelogram.
(c) A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides is a parallelogram.
mastery.solution_text:
(a) A rhombus needs four equal sides, and the adjacent sides of a rectangle may be different lengths.
(a) Sometimes true — only when the rectangle is a square.
(b) A rhombus has four equal sides, which makes both pairs of opposite sides equal and parallel.
(b) Always true.
(c) A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides.
(c) Never true — exactly one pair of parallel sides rules a parallelogram out.

mastery.question_text: Jo is asked to name a quadrilateral that has four equal sides and four right angles. She writes "rhombus" and is marked wrong, with "square" given as the answer. Using the hierarchy, explain why Jo’s answer is not false, and why "square" is the better answer.
mastery.solution_text:
A rhombus is any quadrilateral with four equal sides, and this shape has four equal sides, so calling it a rhombus is a true statement.
The shape also has four right angles, which is more than a rhombus requires.
"Square" is the lowest name in the hierarchy that the shape fits, so it accounts for every property, while "rhombus" leaves the right angles out.
Jo’s answer is true, but it is not the most specific name.

mastery.question_text: Describe a quadrilateral that is a kite but not a rhombus, and a quadrilateral that is a rhombus but not a square. Explain what your two examples show about the direction of the hierarchy.
mastery.solution_text:
A kite with sides $3$ cm, $3$ cm, $7$ cm, $7$ cm has two pairs of equal adjacent sides but not four equal sides, so it is a kite and not a rhombus.
A quadrilateral with four sides of $5$ cm and no right angle has four equal sides, so it is a rhombus and not a square.
Every rhombus is a kite and every square is a rhombus, but neither example works in reverse.
Inclusion runs one way only: the more specific shape has all the properties of the more general one, never the other way round.
